TO THE SPIRIT OF THE AGE. (ATITII APOLOGIES TO MR. AUSTIN DODSON.) If I wbree ibul in moments of reflection, Though criticism may be fair and true,: ) I d not go in too much for vivisection If I were yort.i ; I would not take the flowers of life, and tear them Apart, their inner secrets all to view; I'd pluck them gently, reverently wear them, If I were mu; I d leave some gossamer of tender fancies 'lô life's wide) mea.dovf, gemmed along with dew, Xot sweep tbens all before stern Fact's advances, If I were you. If I were you I'd leave Some twilight hours 'Twist glaring daylight and the night's black hue, Some neutral-tinted scenes—some shady bowers, If I were y-ou. I would not let the oil of toleration— The sameness of one general " width of view" Subdue the free waves' motion to stagnation If I were you. not laugh down enthusiasm's fire As antique and high-flown--I'd leave some few Sparks of a noble rage, a generous ire, 'IfI were you. And 0 ! amid the rush for wealth or pleasure, And all the hurly-burly and to-do, I'd leave some breathing-space, some nooks of leisure, Some time for laying up th'' enduring Treasure, If I were you.

AN ENWASH-AMERICAN ON HOME RULE.

The following interesting communication on Rome Rule is from the pen of Mr. U. U. Barker, formerly editor and joint proprietor of the "Examiner." Mr. Barker now holds a responsible post on one of the largest of the New York papers, and resides in Jersey City, New York t We are kept pretty well posted here by the lead- ing daily papers with the movements made on your side of tha water in respect of the Home Rule ques- tion. When I was on sny "native heath," as you know, my pen and tongue have often been used in demanding that the fullest justice should be dealt out to Ireland, but that the Union should be pre- served at all hazards. If we are not to change our opinions under the influence of increased light and fresh intelligence, then I want to know what in the name of goodness we continue to live for. Well, my years of residence here, far removed from the scene of strife, have put me in a position to judge dispassionately of the question that has vexed Ire-a land and England for centuries, and prevented the consideration and passage of measures having for their object the amelioration of the condition of the whole people. Living here, with the whole country divided into States, and each State possessing its own government, with subjection in important affairs to the chief government at Washington, it is manifest to me that it would be utterly impossible for one parliament to legislate satisfactorily for all sections of the country, as is attempted to be done by Commons, Lords, and Sovereign in the United Kingdom. It is manifest, too, that nothing that the English Parliament can do will satisfy the Irish, short of Home Rule. It is of no use attempting to give to a people that which it does not want or value, and this has been proved over and over again with Englishmen, much less with Irishmen. I have by degrees grown to the opinion that, as sure as the sun shines, Ireland will be conceded Home Rule as a matter of policy and in the interests of England herself. I have no more love for the Irish than I ever had, but I want to act up to the principle of giving to the devil his due. The whole of the Irish people, save the hair-brained Orange partisans, who are as great mad caps as the ultra ribbon men, are imbued with the determination to give no rest or quiet until Home Rule shall be granted; and this is only the position the repealers of the Corn Laws, the advocates of the ballot, the claimants for the extension of the franchise, etc., assumed in England in past days. The Irishman, however, must have a grievance, and, yet, when you come down to the bed rock of facts, the Englishman is not one whit more contented than the Irishman if he has not a grievance: and he is jast as ready as Paddy to magnify a political trifle into a mountain, when op- portunity serves. Both in the interests of Ireland and England, I would, had I the power, adopt heroic and pro- nounced remedies for curing this Irish sore, and I have astonished many Irishmen here by telling them how acute the application should be. My position is this, and I have heard the same view expressed by other Englishmen here who, in the old country, were Tories of the NoSurrender School, but who have, by residence here, grown more con-

The Crofters Act provided that in the case of a crskttest inaking an applica- tion to the Commissioner with reVebee to tbilarnotpt; :Of his rent, or his arrears of rent, all ,proceedings for' his removal should be stayed till such a time as the applica- tion was adjudioated upon, but* undeif! another section any crofter who became a bankrupt was deprived of the benefit of the Act. Therefore it was possible for anV landlord who wished to take proceedings against his crofter tenant to exclude him from the protraction of the Actby making him a banlcruptsbnt it was only fair to eV , that the landlords had on the whole acted towards their ' crofters with the utmost forbearance. Under this bill the „Crofters' Commission would have 'power to prohibit timeviotion of a eroftertill his application fkor the fixing of a fair rent had been decided, and if the landlord took proceedings the croftercoutd make antapplioation to the Commission for protection, and they -would therefore inquire into his ability to pay the arream of 'rent or a certain proportion of the claim.---The Duke of ARGYLL willingly.i acquiesed arthe passing: of the bill, which in truth did nothing more than carry into effect the object and intention of the Crofters Act. ; At the same time there was evidence ~thatscrnfters had been \with,- holding nnt which they were perfectly able to pay, • and lad been tcpuinulating &LOCI( and tpetirliftg money r .boats—The hill was r,e,i'damecoud time. The Police Force Entranciasement Jul passed through Committee. .") THE IRISH 'LAND.,I3ILL. Upon the motion for the House to be again In Com.' mittee on the Irish Land Law Bill,• . The Duke of ABERCORN, while anxiouSto afford eveiv facility tcr: the Government :for the passing of the bill, appealed to the Prime ,Minister to allow it to be corn- , mitted pro forma that evening,-so that the new equitable jurisdiction clauses might be introduced. Lord Ftrzounatn joined in the appeal, as did-also Earl GRANVILLE, wha doubted whether anything would be gained by taking the unusual course of discussing the remodelled clauses, and recommitting the :bill afterwards. The Marquis of SALISBURY would have preferred to have heard the clauses discussed, but in deference to what appeared to be the aeneral feeling of the House, adopted the'noble Duke's suggestion. He proposed that they should go through the bill pro forma, inserting the Government amendment', and such other amendments ns they might be prepared to accept, without discussion, and that the bill should be re-committed. The House went into 'Como:IRLO pro forma, and the new clauses and amendments having been intro- duced, the re-committal was fixed,for Monday, the 13th of June. "The County Courts Consolidation Bill was read a second time. Rants Consurraa.—On the motion of Lord CRAN- BRoo4o, Select Committee was appointed to inquire into and report upon the subject of rabies in dogs and the laws applicable thereto. THE COERCION Bite,.—The House then went into Corot ruittee on the Crimes Bill, and resumed the consideration V. clause 2. The first amendment moved by Mr. Ilealy—a proposal that the offence of taking part in conspiracy should be made to read "wilt ullv or knowingly taking part "—was resisted by Mi. Balfour githout further argument than that the words proposed' would not make the'bill dearer or more certain.' The Chief Secretary declining to give any more satisfactory reply. Mr. HEALY moved to report pro- grew, and a third division was taken on that question, the numbers being 253 to 114. A fourth division followed en the amendment itself and showed that the majority now numbered only 155 to 114. Discussion could therefore pro- ceed without further fear in the meantime of closure which requires the majority to be 290 when the majority is over 40 —An important amendment by, Sir C. RUSSELL to define tbe conspiracy offence as " conspiring by violence or intimidation," instead of "taking part in any criminal conspiracy," as it stands in the bill, was after dis- cussion negatived by 237 to 165 votes, and an amendment by Mr. RBID to lessen the stringency of the enb.section under discussion was defeated by 265 to 180.—Progress was reported soon after one o'clock, after which hour the Irish members raised on the report of Supply a discussion on the proclamation of meetings in Ulster.—The House continued itting till a late hour. •

LW THE QUEEN'S PRIZE AT WIHELEDON.—The total aggre- gate value of the Queen's Prize competition at Wimble- don in the ensuing meeting will amount to £2,220, of which the first £250 will be given day her Majesty, the winner also, as on previous occasions, receiving the gold medal and badge of the National Rifle Association. In all 400 prizes will be given in the competition. The completed returns just received from the Wesleyan District Connexions give the full accredited membership of churches as 412,311, a decrease of 63 on the previous year; the trial membership as 31,416 • juniors, 52,780; the latter being an increase of nearly 8,000; and candi- dates for the ministry, 106. These numbers will be pre- sented to the Wesleyan Conference at Manchester in July. A letter from the Archbishop of Canterbury was read, in which the Primate said that the double :Object of the association, namely, to simplify funeral and mourning ceremonial, and to encourage burial in perishable coffins in the simple earth, had hiS full concurrence and sympathy. Kezialt Westwood., 15, of Coseley, was on Monday com- mitted for trial for wounding Allen Bellingham, a watch- man in the employ of Lord Dudley. It waa alleged that Bellingham detected prisoner in the act of stealing coal, and upon chasing him prisoner said he would cut Iris eye out. JAMMED TO DEAT7I.—A shocking accident occurred at the Arley Mine, Bottom Place, Wigan, on Saturday after- noon, by which a man named John M'Custring, residing in Adelaide-street, Wigan, was jammed to death. On the waggons being uncoupled he was found quite dead. He leaves a widow and six young children. CURRENT POLITICS. Mr. W. O'Brien, editor, of rrkited Ireland, WAS on Monday nominated for the„representation of North-East Cork. He was, proposed by the Rev. Canon Wigmore, P.P., seconded by Mr. Wm. Fitzgerald, solicitor. There being no other' candidate, he was declared duly elected, in the 'mote of Mr.-Ed. Leamy. • -AI Swansea telegram states that Mr. Gladstone has accepted an invitation of Sir Hussey Vivian, M.P., to ,spend the latter portion of the Whitsuntide recess at Singleton Abbey, Swansea. Mr. Gladstone will make no public engagements except the reception of addresses of welcome from the inhabitants of South Wales. Lord Hartington called at the Foreign Office on Monday afternoon, and remained for over half-an-hour in consul- tation with Lord Salisbury, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Goschen. It is understood that his lordship called by appointment, the Government desiring to have the benefit of his views upon the present position and prospects of the Crimes Bill; and upon the Government amendments to the Land Bill, with which they had been informed a considerable namber of Liberal Unionist members of the House of Common's had expressed dissatisfaction. The results of yesterday's conference were satisfactory, to the Govern- ment.

It is stated that the Liberal Unionists are organising.a series of important meetings for the Whitsuntide recess. ,The most noteworthy-of these will be a conference and mass meeting in connection with the National Radical Unten at Birmingham, at which Mr. Chamberlain will preside, and a great meeting at Manchester, which will probably be addressed by Lord Hartington. The Bir- mingham meetings will be held on June the Ist., the public meeting being held in the Tow; HalL The Glad- stonians are also making preparations for an anti-coercion campaign, in which Mr. J. Morley and other leading mem- bers of the party will take part.

THE EIGHTY Ctrs —A meeting of the Eighty Club was held on Wednesday evening to consider a grievance of the Unionist members,stated in a motion that it was inexpedient that the principal guests at the dinners of the club should be selected from one section only of the Liberal party. This was met by an amendment expressing confidence in the com- mittee and in the Irish policy of the Liberal party. After a warm discussion, the amendment was carried by 143 votes to 55. The Unionists minority afterwards met ;under the presidency of Lord Northbrook, and decided to withdraw from the club.

r THE OATHS BILL.—LETTER FROM LORD R. CHURCHILL, In 'new of the notice given by Mr. Tomlinson, M.P., that he will move the rejection of the Oaths Bill, the following extract from a letter from Lord R. Churchill to the Rev. F. G. Lee, Vicar of Lambeth, will be read 'with special interest "The Oaths Bill now before the House of Commons gives to members, as I read it, the option either of mak- ing an affirmation or of taking and subscribing the oath. " Under these circux.stances I confess I do not see how the Bill can be with propriety opposed by those who took action adverse to Mr. Bradlaugh in 1880 and the succeed. jug years. "IC Mr. Bradlaugh's original claim to affirm had been legal no opposition could have been offered. It was, however, found to be illegal. "The Parliamentary opposition to him was based upon ,the profanation of the oath, arising from its being taken by a nerson notoriously without religious belief. This bill, if passed, puts an end to such profanation, and opposition to this bill must tend to throw much doubt upon the reality and sincerity of the action of those who prevented Mr. Bradlaugh from taking the oath in the Parliament of 1880.

"I may be toll that'a similar bill was opposed and de- feated in 1883, but that bill was introduced and sup- ported for the purpose of evading or circumventing the decision of Parliament adverse to Mr. 13radlaugh. It was essentially a • Privilegium; and was commonly called a • Bradlaugh `Relief 11111, Mr. Bradlaugh was out of the House, and the bill proposed to alter. the general law in Order to get him into the !louse. • "The circumstances attendant upon the present bill are essentially different. Mr. Bradlaugh, having taken the oath under the ruling of Mr. Speaker, is in the House. No person, no action, in respect of his taking the oath can interfere with him; as far as regards his own personal position as a member of Parliament he requires no relief by alteration of the general law, he derives no special or Immediate benefit from the bill now under consideration.

"All this being so, I am strongly of opinion that the hands of those who, like myself, were identified with opposition to• Mr. Bradlaugh in a former Parliament are teed. Should we oppose aeid defeat- the trill we by no means exclude blr. Bradlaug,h from Parliament ; all we do is .that we provide that the oath shall be continually pro- faned whenever Mr. Bradlaugh or persons of similar opinions are • elected as members of the House of Commons. ",By supporting and passing the bilL on the otherhand, we secure that the Parliamentary oath in the future will in all probability only be taken by those who believe in and who revere its effective solemnity. The right hon. baronet's open- ing remarks, in which he declared himself an earnest Liheral and spoke of reunion, were most enthusiastically applauded. Were they, be asked, in May, 1887, to say that they would iodefiiiieely defer satisfying Ireland's sentiments and aspirations and support a Coercion Bill, which in Jens, 1885, they would not have looked at, not because there had been any outburst of crime since, but be-, cause some sensation had been get up in the newspapers about crimes which were committed five years ago 7 In replying to a vote of thanks for his statesmanlike address. Sir George Trevelyan said that the reunion of the Liberal party was the one object of his life, and his firm opinion was that to that reunion there was no real public obstacle. Advices received at Dundee by a mail steamer state that owing to bad fishing in North Ice/and, whose popu- lation subsists mostly on fish, five persons have died this winter from sheer starvation, owing to the straits caused by the failure in the fishing and hay crops last season. Hundred have arranged to emirate •to America. The weather in Faroe has been so ban that fishing is almost a failure. SERIOUS RAILw.4r EICCIDENT.—A collision occurred on the Caledonian Railway early on Saturday morning, near Gretna, owing to the end of a heavy goods train breaking away upon an incline. The first part of the train was pulled up, and the detached waggons ran into it with such force that twenty of the latter were thrown off the rails and wrecked, seven being pitched over the embank- ment. No person was injured, and, after a few hours' delay the line was cleared. On Saturday Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone gave a.garden party at Donis Hill, to which the delegates attending the Colonial Conference were specially invited. Lord Gran- ville and Mr. and Mrs. Childers were also among the guests. In the evening Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone drove into town, and dined with Sir Lyon 'and Lady Playfair. The Earl and Countess Spenceef Sir George and Lady Trevelvan, Mr. and Mrs. Childers, and Mr. James Russell Lowell were amongst the company. At the Bolton Comity Sessions, on Monday, judg- ment was given in an important colliery case, the Home Secretary v. Herbert Fletcher, owner of the Ladyshord Colliery, Little Lever. The defendant refused to Stop • the use of naked lights, and use safety lamps, as ordered by an umpire appointed in an arbitration, and the ques- tion for decision was whether, under a saving clause of the act, the defendant had taken remedial measures or not. The magistrates fined defendant £2O and costs. DEA= OF Ms. T. COOPE J.P..„ OF WIGAN. The death is announced of dr. Timothy Coope, J.P., Wigan, wnich occurred on Sunday, at Wichita, in the United States. 'The deceased gentleman was the prin- cipal of the firm of Coope and Co., the well-known manufacturing clothiers of Wigan,and, when in England, lived at Bethany House, Mornington-road, Southport. For some time past Mr. Coope, who was about seventy years of age, had been in ill-health, and the tour through the United States was undertaken for the purpose of recruiting himself. He was a Liberal in politics, and belonged to the Methodist body known as the Church of Christ; but he took a warm interest in all kinds of re- ligious work, and was proprietor of the Christian Common- wealth. J the - notorious James Carey, who was shot by O'Connel, is believed to be safe in Ihe colonies. He was generally re- ,garded in Dublin, before the Plicenix Park trials, as a sober, honest, clever, and hard-working artisan,who paid no attention to anything outside his business. It is stated that Farrell, the van driver, is also getting on well. Re is now in the colonies, but previous to his departure he spent some time in disguise in England. EXTRAORDINARY DISCOVERY IN A COAL PIT.—An extraordinary discovery was made on Saturday after- noon in the mining neighbourhood of Troedyrhiw, in the Merthyr Valley. As some miners were crossing the Cwmfelin Mountain they were attracted to the mouth of an abandoned coal-pit shaft, from which piercing cries were proceeding. They immediately communicated with the police, and a band of miners was organised and lowered into the shaft by ropes. On reaching the bottom, a depth of about sixteen feet, a little well-dressed girl was found lying on her back comparatively uninjured. The child was brought to the surface and conveyed to Dr. Jones's surgery, and the doctor certified that she had sustained no injuries beyond slight bruises on the head. It is supposed that the infant was thrown into the pit, 'but how she escaped with her life is marvellous. The bottom of the shaft consist& of rocks strewn with debris, 'find the carcases of a dog and sheep, on which it is sup- posed the child alighted. On Alonday, at Merthyr, Miriam Jones, aged about it, was remanded on a charge of attempting to murder her illegitimate child. The -accused was seen in the neighbcfnrhood with a child, and after being traced and arrested she admitted that she had.droppedthe infant down the pit.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMM ONS.-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMM ONS.-TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the Chair' at four o'clock. POSTAL DEFICIT.— The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHE- QUER announced a deficit in post-office and telegraph ac- eounts owing to increased capital expenditure reinkred necessary by parcel post and sixpenny telegram arrange- ments. COLONIAL KING-HARMAN'S GUESTS. The House heard with much Interest an interrogation of Mr. Stuart 'Wortley by Sir W. LAWSON as to the prolongation of et Margate licensed vlctuiller's dinner at Cliftonville Hotel beyond the hours of licensed houses through the bospitable.collu- slop of Colonel King-Harman. It appeared that on the festive occasion it was discovered that a musical programme could not be concluded before eleven O'clock. and that an extension of time had not been applied for to the magis- trates. Colonel King-Harman, who was staying at the hotel, got out of tbe difficulty by making the whole meet- ing his guests without any •hjection from the local super-, intendant, who was present. TIIE JuEILEE FINEWORES.—Mr. Stuart elicited from the Secretary ef State for War the fact that pyrotechnists had been asked to submit a programme of fireworks for a Jubilee celebration in the parks, but the Government bad decided that there should be no fireworks, and this decision was announced to the ,fire-work makers at once by tile graph. Trrn Lama BscarrAny.—The now customary tibsence of the Chief Secretary to the Lord-Lientenant of Ireland at the question hour gave rise toeinte angry comment when 'Mr. Dillon found that he:conld get DO information as to the ,policy of proclaiming an anti-Home Rule meeting at Dun- gannon. Mr. Balfour came in during the hubbub, and wits greeted With ironical cheers. His presence did not add to the information of the House, inasmuch as Mr. Balfour asked for notice of the question put to him. MORE JUBILEB.—The First Lord of the Treasury, who wore the wedding favour presumably received at the mar- riage of the Prime Minieter's son, moved "That in celebra- tion of the fiftieth year of her Majesty's reign this House will attend at the Church Of St. Margaret's, Westminster, on Sunday next, the '22nd ef May."—Mr. GLADSTONE se- conded the motion, which was passed, with one critical observation from Mr. HEALY as to the deplorable circum- -.dance that the Jubilee should be signalised by a " Jubilee ,Coercion Bill." THE •COERCION BILL. 'The night was devoted to the consideration of the •Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill in Committee, the sprincipal topic of discussion being Sir W. Harcourt's pro- posed proviso to the first.clause to-secure that no private inquiry should be held into matters relating to public meet- ings or transactions relating to the letting, luring, or the 'dealing with, working for, or hiring of any persons in the ordinary course of trade. business, or occupation. The smendmeet was designed, its author said, to elicit from the Government an answer to the question whether they were willing to give to the tenants of Ireland the same protec- tion that had been given to the labourers of England by the trades union legislation of 1875. The Government resisted the amendment, Mr. BALFOUR stating that the bill would not be worth going on with if it were to exclude from its Operation the offence of conspiracy to boycott.—Mr. Glad- stone and the Attorney-General took part in the debate, the latter raising a look of astonishment and a smile an many faces by' the innocent observation that dictionaries would chow that the word boycotting had not been invented twenty-five, "or at least twenty years" ago! The division took place shortly before eleven o'clock, when the amend- ment was negatived by 242 to 180 voter, majority 82. Other amendrnents were considered, the Committee again sitting very late. -

_ HOUSE OF COMMONS w EDNESOAIr. • The Spiker took the chair at 20 minutes after 12 o'clock. • , THE COERCION BILL In committee on the Crimes Bill the House proceeded with the consideration of tbe second clause, which extends the power of +dealing summarily with persons in proclaimed districts. Several amendments having been rejectio, some by narrow majorities, a proposal to secure the prosecution of rfotere In t /later was accepted by the Government Upon a proposal that in prosecutions under the clause intknated by Crown officials the fiat of the Attorney Gemral should first be obtained, the closure was moved by Mr. Smith, and was agreed to without a divison •, and upon the amendment being put it was rejected by 219 to 145. Mr. terraw-Lireavnit moved the rejection of the sub-section of the clause which defined as an offender under the Act any person who ebould take part in any criminal conspiracy to compel or induce any , person either not to fulfil his legal obligations, or not let, hire, use, or eccupy any • land or not to deal with, work for, or hire any persdn in the ordinary course of trade, business, or occupation, or to interfere with the administra- tion of the law. He moved this on the ground that the sub=section withdrew a large class of the most important cases under the law of conspiracy+from the superior eourts In order to submit them to the resident magistrates, a tri- bunal wholly incompetent to deal with them. Mr. Straw- LEFEVRE contended that in case the section passed in its present form the tenants could not continue to resist unfair rents, and that the section was, in fact, one to enable land- lords to collect rents by a new process. The ATTOILNEY GENERAL for IBEIAND argued that the clause was direc- ted. not against innocent combinations, but against crimi- nal combinations. The closure was then applied by Ma- jority of 87 in a House of :373 members. By the time the 'division bad been taken .a quarter to Six bad been reached, and the point was raised whether the amendment could then be put. The Chairman decided, amidst, pretests from the Irish members, that a division could be taken, as the ,:lobate upon the subject had,heen closed arid it therefore 'Was net oppose,' business. At five minutes past six the Inumbers in the division were declared under furthee protest I the result being that the amendment was rejected by 223 to 41113. Progress was then reported. I The House ndjourned at nine minutes past six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THORSDAY. Whe.Speaker to6k the chair at 40 ASNEXSTION OF ZOLULAND.-Bir H. HOLLAND, who was qesestioned respecting the annexation of Zululand, said it would not be annexed to Natal, but would be administered as a.Crown colony for the benefit of the natives. The ter- ritory annexed included the kingdom of Cetewayo, except .what .had.beec assigned to the now Republic, and the area was 2:800 Square miles, so that, incl lading the Reserve, the area ‘e British-territory was 8,220 square miles. It was proposed to grant pensions for life to the chiefs. He had no moon to believe Neat there was any body of pinion in S.,uthWrica adveme to the recent extension.

EXTRAORDINARY IRPOgrrtox.—Mr. ilsammair called at- tention to e rematkable case of imposition, in which a pension of £4O a year of a Custom-house official who re- tired in 1845 at the age of 67, and died in 1652, had been drawn by his wife for 20 years after his death, and for a further 12 years by his daughter, up to March last.—Mr. CALEB WEIGHT affirmed that there were several cases of a milar character—Mr. JJ-GXSON replied that in the case re- ferred to the offender was prosecated, convicted of felony, and sentenced to a term of imprisonment. TDE QUEEN'S Trrus,—Mr. Smrrn, replying to4nestions, stated that at the Colonial Conference there had been some discussion on the subject of recognising the progress made by the colonies during Her Majesty's reign by a forth.... ex- tension of the Royal titks, and inquiries had been sent out to the Governors of the Colonies as to their views on the question, but the answers had not yet been received. div.head: -THE EXAMINER,
div.p: -THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY 21, 1887

tj SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN is a Liberal ll oionist ; but if all Liberal Unionists were ji" him there Fould soon cease to be a split 11 the Liberal party. He has made two im- trant speeches during the week; one on otic)rlday, as guest of the Eighty Club; and the erer on Wednesday at the Manchester toth")rin Club—speeches so conciliatory in th:e. so thoughtful and yet so patriotic, that ttls'Y cannot but have great influence over I ,oderate-minded men of all sections of the Zberal party, who are anxious that the breach 1,1.°111d be closed which threatens to grow thlder and wider. Sir GEORGE rightly thinks „at the Liberal Unionists who have allied , ill'rnselves with the Tories "stand at this tat°,,„lllerit on the least stable ground as a sepa- tit; Party." He has no sympathy with trals who, because they cannot have their 1)4 way, go outside the ranks of their own thoi and thus make bad worse. Answering do ht Who ask what the Dissentients were to ....e says : 'LA f - kasis: -rue policy of the Liberal Unionists was to th„, , on a settlement of the Irish question which tu thl'd be free from the main objections that they Rt7insoelves felt, but which should be bold, thorough, er ‘qe t us' and final. They should have made the p anee of such a settlement and its embod- -4; i t n the statute book, at least the price of their Ntlilli)iort to the Conservative party, and since they d not get that, they ought to have made to, Is they can make it to-morrow, and ought Vile condition of continuing that support. would, we grant, have been an intern- and consistent line of action, and, if it . .Lt"ei been pursued, Parliament would have tttl occupied to-day, not as it is in passing tt Worst Coercion Bill that this country has Ite' known but in framing a measure of kit)llle R ' • v.: . Rule which would in all probability tittf given peace to Ireland, and have been ,I.l4rtDtable to the bulk of the people of the 4t, tcl Kingdom. The Liberal Unionists 1 4,'Ottea,,Pt to complain that they have been ,?..„- into an attitude of hostility to 1re- ,(4114.t'1l to the Liberal party by the harsh 4 18"„ which have been said of them: but tptorl *"clor statesmanship which is founded k retaliation : and why should Ireland ado to suffer because English Liberals
Illeral
lOrt' e-d•

leaders of the Nationalist party by endeavour- ing to associate them with crime in Ireland. If it could be shown that there was strong evidence in support of the .presumption that the Parnellites had been privy to outrage and murder, Englishmen would, with one voice, irrespective of party, say—" We will not be patty to placing the government of Ireland in the hands of these men." But the evidence is all the other way; Lord SPENCER, Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN, Sir W. HARCOURT, and Mr. GLADSTONE, all speaking from official experience, are unanimous in declaring that they have no reason to believe the Irish leaders have been:connected with the crimes that have been committed in Ireland. The furious indignation" which the Conserva- tives have displayed against the Irish mem- bers has been, as Sir GEORGE says, " put on for the occasion." It is a sham, and nobody knows this better than Lord Starsnuss—and that, too, even when he accuses Mr. GLAD- STONE of having "an ally tainted with the strong presumption of conniving at assassina- tion." The fact is, as Sir GEORGE TRE- VELYAN points out, the very same charge was brought in the very same language against Mr. PARNELL by Mr. FORSTER ; and yet Lord SALISBURY and his party, after it was made, went down on their knees to the Irish leaders in order to secure the Irish vote. They promised Home Rule, and they prom- ised to abandon the Criminal Law Amend- ment Act, if the Irish would vote Tory. And is it not a matter of history that Lord CARNAR- VON, as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, had con- ferences with Mr. PARNELL, with Lord SALIS- BURY'S knowledge and sanction? The Tories secured the Irish vote ; they were returned to office on the strength of it; and now, within two years of the alliance, they scoff at Home Rule, bring in a Coercion Bill, and de- nounce their former supporters as men who foster crime and connive at assassination. But it won't do; the Tories have been guilty of a base betrayal of the Irish party; and they are now adding insult to injury in a way which shows that they are lost to all sense of shame, and have become cruel and unscrupu- lous to the last degree. And to think that Lord HARTINGTON, JOSEPEI CHAMBERLAIN, and JOHN BRIGHT can join hands with such base time-servers! 'Tis enough to make the angels weep.

A strong deputation ot over a score of nit- brow women, and a large number of their friends, waited upon the HOME SECRETARY, on Tuesday, in reference to the proposal to amend the Mines Regulation Bill by pro hibiting the employment of female labour at the pit brow. It is due to the Govern- ment to say that the suggested restriction does not proceed from them • it is proposed by miners representatives in the interests, as they allege, of the women themselves. Mr. ATHERLEY JONES'S amendment to the Mines Regulation Bill is in effect a total prohibi- tion of female labour in connection with mines. Mr. BURT does not go so far as this in the first instance. He proposes to get rid of pit-brow women by degrees by making it a penal offence to engage them for the future. The present hands would be allowed to work, but no new hands would be taken on. We must confess that we have not seen a single good reason alleged for a restriction of this kind. Mr. BURT himself admits that the pit-brow women are thoroughly honest and virtuous, so that the question of morality, which formed such an important consideration when it was decided to prohibit the employment of women below ground, does not come in on this occasion. It is true that they have to work hard, and that their attire is not at- tractive; but if Parliament is to interfere on such grounds as these, it will never have any- thing else to do, and what little it does will be in every respeet mischievous. It is not suggested that the labour is unhealthy, and, as the women like the work, and are fairly well paid, it would on the face of it be unjust to deprive them of this means of obtaining an honest livelihood. As things go in these days of sentimentalism and high pres- sure education, there is a tendency to shirit work which happens to soil the hands. We have already too many fine ladies who are not worth their salt either indoors or out; and we ought rather to help than to hinder a class of women who believe that their hands and arms were made to take a share of the world's work. We may be mistaken, but we somehow suspect that the miners are thinking more of their own interests than of the interests of their "sisters, cousins, and aunts," in the attempt which is being made to prohibit female labour at the pit brow. The women compete with the men, and competition tends to bring down the price of labour as of other commodities. Granted that, for a time at any rate, wages would increase if no more women were to be seen at the pit brow, the question still remains—is this just to the , women? What if the women were to organ- ise, and demand that no person of the other 1 sex under 2 1 years of age should be Permit- I ted to work in connection with a mine? They ; would doubtless be able to show that a reduction of this kind would have a good effect in increasing wages by stimulating the demand for female labour. But the young men would not like it; they would feel that Parliament was cruelly interfering with their ; right to earn a living. We are glad to see ' that Mr. MATTHEWS, the Home Secretary, ex- , pressed his sympathy with the views of the! Deputation, and promised, on behalf of the Government, to resist the prohibitive clauses which it is proposed to introduce into the Mines Regulation Bill. The fact seems to be, as Mr. KAY, president of the St. Helens: Mines Association stated, that the miners of the far north, where this movement has had: its origin, do not understand the pit-brow ' question as it affects Lancashire. But Lanca- shire has spoken, and Lancashire in this matter will have her way. The objectionable amendments may be moved when the bill comes before the House of Commons, but we are quite sure that they will never become I law.

YOUTHFUL - POACHERS AT BURTONWOOD.— At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, John Herrop, Thomas Stokes, Thomas English, Joseph Mullen, John Phillips, Thomas Price, and William Downes, boyswhose ages ranged from 15 to 16, were charged with having on Sunday, the 24th ult., been on land at Burtonwood, in the occupation of Henry Bent, for the purpose of searching for game. A similar charge against a boy named Owen Holland was withdrawn on his consenting to give evidence for the prosecution. Mr. Riley, solicitor, of St. Helens, appeared for the defence. Evidence was given by Samuel Lloyd, who is in the employ of Mr. Bent, who proved seeing the boys with two fox terrier dogs with them in a field belonging to Mr. Bent. The dogs killed a rabbit. The boys, who had no ferrets with them, were close to. When they saw him they ran. He chased them, and caught Hol- land. Owen Holland said he, along with the other boys, went for a walk; and when passing the field— which was near the:road, and in which was a pond —they saw a rat, and one of the dogs went after it, the'other one running round to the other side. Just then a rabbit jumped up, and the dogs pursued it and caught it. It was then that the last witness came up. By Mr. Riley: They did not follow to see the dogs kill the rabbit, but to call them off. The lads were each fined is and costs.

The Government have provided £17,000 for a Jubilee service in Westminster Abbey; but they cannot see their way to seventeen pence for fireworks. The people are per- mitted to find the money, but they are not to have a share in the fun. •

Mr. Justice Day, on Tuesday, ordered the " cat " to be administered to a thrice-con- victed ruffiAn who had been guilty of robbery with violence. This is the right way to treat offenders of this kind. If the rascal's con- science cannot be reached, it is at any rate possible t• get at his back, and teach him that there are cases in which the fear of the law is the beginning of wisdom.

There was some good" gagging" by the Opera Ciimoany which was at the Warring- ton Public Hall this week. One " character, ' on being sneered at as a farm servi.nt, in- stantly answered, "Farm servants are some- body now-a-days ; I am chairman of the Prim- rose League in this district "—a neat hit at the way things are done now which took the fancy of the audience, and evoked a roar of laughter.

Tuesday night's " Gazette " contains a Royal proclamation prescribing the designs for the various coins issued by the Royal Mint, including a five-pound piece, a two-pound piece, and a new coin to be called a double florin, of the value of 4.5. All that is now needed to make everybody happy is another Royal proclamation decreeing that for the future the weekly wages of all her Majesty's subjects shall be paid in five•pound pieces.

The Ship Canal Company expand in their views as they find the money coming in. At first the high-water mark for the district was three millions sterling ; now it is fixed at four. It was originally suggestei that the Prince of Wales should be asked to cut the first sod ; now it is proposed that the Queen herself should be solicited to take part in the celebration. Nothing succeeds like success, and we shall all he ready in a month or two to shout—" Hurrah for the Ship Canal I"

It seems that there is a portion of the Coercion Bill which not even the Liberal Unionists can swallow, and they can swallow almost anything. At a meeting of that body held yesterday, it was resolved that Lord Hartitagton should inform the Govern- ment that they could not support the clause under which it is proposed to bring Irish prisoners to England for trial. The Government will of course do as they are told, and "drop it." How pleasant it must be for the Government!

A treat consisting of the three T's—Tea, Toast, and Tattle—seems to be the stock thing for the Jubilee celebration ; but the people of Newton and Earlestown have set their hearts on something more. They have no park or recreation ground ; and they have reason to believe that if they will speak nicely to the lord of the manor he will grant them land forthe purpose. Let us hope that he will ; it will do him and them good; and besides, "Jubilee Park" has a pleasant ring with it.

The Warrington Chamber of Commerce is a useful institution, but its views would have more weight if its meetings were not as a rule so ridiculously small. According to report there were four persons in attendance (includ- ing the president and secretary) at a general meeting " which was held on Mon- day. Four Well, that is one more than the three tailors of Tooley- street ; but it leaves room for improvement in the matter of attend- ance. Members who were not present on Monday, please to take the hint.

Mr. John Crosfield is doing a handsome thing in inviting Sunday and day school teachers and pupil teachers, along with wives and husbands, to Walton Lea on the Monday of Jubilee week. Our neutral " contem- porary twits him with not subscribing to the Jubilee Fund. A reference of this kind is charmingly graceful, seeing that the " neutral " itself is not yet down for as much as a brass farthing. Nor has it under- taken to entertain anybody. Perhaps, poor thing, it regards its " neutrality" as sufficiently entertaining.

I Widnes did itself honour on Monday by I opening a Free Library. It is a Free Lending Library, of course, and this was revealed in the opening ceremony. Mr. F. H. Gossage, as chairman of the Local Board, applied for : a book, having filled up the required forms I for a free borrower, and the book was handed ' to him by Professor Rendall, of the Liverpool University College. who had been asked to open the Library. This is better—far better— than the way they have in Warrington.

' In the course of his address Professor Ren- dall made the following suggesti‘'re remarks, which may be commended to the attention of the Warrington Library Committee:—" He thought there was nothing more contemptible and stupid than the act of a miser storing up his gold, and going about starved and and naked and miserable, whilst he was rich, if he knew the secret that that gold would buy all he waned. And so, if we permitted the treasures that had been left for ages to lie on the shelves, and used them not, we were in the same pitiable state that the miser was in respect to his wealth!! .

The Liverpool Church of England Work- ing Men's Society have communicated with the Prime Minister, and the leader of the House of Commons, with reference to the im- prisonment of the Rev. J. Bell Cox; and they have had. answer. Lord Salisbury and Mr. Smith both intimate that "the Crown has no power to release persons far con- tempt ; " and Mr. Smith adds that the proce- dure does not admit of the exercise of the Queen's prerogative. This is cold comfort. The reverend Ritualist has got himself in gaol, and it would seem that he will have to get himself out.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, James Unsworth, a shopkeeper, of South- worth-with-Croft, was fined zos for selling pepper containing three per cent of adultera- tion. It was admitted that Unsworth was not supposed to be guilty of the adulteration, and it seems hard that he should be brought before the magistrates. It was suggest,,d that the grinder of the pepper was at fault, and that the adulteration was so much waste from the grindstones. Now if that grinder could only be placed between the upper and nether mill- stone, he would have an eye to the waste, and there would be less adulteration. But you must catch your. grinder before you can squeeze him.

The Mayor of Limerick (Mr. O'Keefe) informed the Mu- nicip4l Council of that city on Thursday that he intended to give "a firm and dignified refusal" to the Lord Chem- herlain's invitation to the Jubilee celebration service in Westminster Abbey.

GALE AT WIDNES AND RIINCOEN.—On Thursday night and yesterday a gale of great severity, accompanied by heavy rain and hMI storms, swept over the districts of Run• corn and Widnes. The tide commenced te flow at Runcorn an hour before the stipulated time, and rose to a height of several feet above that recorded in the tide table. In both towns slates and chimney pots were dislodged in great pro- fusien, while in the early morning shutters were strewn about the parapets in various Portions of the towns. The high wall at the corner of Mersey-street, Runcorn, which was surmounted by a high boarding belonging to Mr. Shepherd, the bill poster, was levelled to the ground, and the expense cf its re-erection will he considerable. The most serious effect of the storm occurred in Milton-road, Widnes, where at an early hour yesterday morning the window of the bedroom of the house occupied by Constable Worsfold was blown completely in, to the great alarm and discomfort of the occupants of the room. In the same road the gable ends of two houses partly collapsed under the pressure of the wind, and but for the kindness of neighbours the inhabitants would have been in a most awkward pre- dicament. So far as can be ascertained no injury to life or limb has occurred in the neighbourhood. EARL OF CHESTER'S RIFLES, RONOORN.—GOLD MEDAL COMPETITION.—The second competition was held on Sat- Inlay. Ford for the respondents. Miss Allcard who is now a Roman Catholic, is the daughter of a gentleman who was the second Mayor of Warring- ton, and who in 1847 unsuccessfully contested the representation of that borough in the Liberal inter- est, his successful opponent being Sir (then Mr.) Gil- bert Greenall. Miss Allcard is between forty and fifty years of age. Under her fathers will, behaving died in 1861,she was entitled to £Bool3absolutely. Secondly she was entitled to a further sum of the same amount for life, with a power of disposition by will only; and thirdly, she was entitled to the income arising from £5,000, over which she had no power of disposition at all ; and on the death of her mother she will be entitled to a further sum. In 1868 she was introduced to Mr. Nihill. who was 'vicar of Si. Mark's Finsbury.. He was then found- ing with Miss Skinner the sisterhood of which Miss Allcard in that year became an associate. After an interval of 18 months, she formally joined the sister- hood and bound herself to it. She made a will. land presented gifts amounting to a large sum to the convent, in accordance with the vow of poverty which was taken by the sisters. In 1871 she be- came a full member of the sisterhood for life, and eight years later, becoming dissatisfied, left it, and almost immediately joined the Church of Rome. Subsequently she commenced anaction against Miss Skinner, the mother superior of the sisterlmod, for the return of the gifts of money, on the ground that when they were made she was acting under undue influence. The ease lasted several days before Mr. Justice Kekewich, the result being that her action was dismissed with costs, and judgment was given for Miss Skinner. ..4aainst this decision Miss All- card now appeals. The hearing of the appeal was resumed on Monday and Tuesday, and their lord- ships reserved judgment.

CORRESPONDENT. Under date may 13th the Rev. R. G. Hughes, Con- gregational.minister, Widnes,. addressed thy follow- ing letter to the Right lion. Joseph Chamberlain, :--•• Dear sir,—A correspondent in Wet Hen- frewshire wrote to Mr. John Bright, soliciting his opinion on the Times and Parnellism.' Assuming that you have seen Mr. Bright's reply to his lettor, might I ask whether you also hold the same view as he on this matter? Does this particular state- ment commend itself to your judgment that all charges of the Times' consist of evidence con- tributed by the rebel conspirators themselves.'" IA , reply Mr. Hughes has received the following letter: —"4O, Princes Gardens, S.W., Mery /6th, 1887. Sir, Mr. Chamberlain has your letter of the 13th inst, and desires me to inform you that his views on the sub- ject referred to were expressed in his last speech at Glasgow, and he has nothing to add to what he then said.—l am, yours obediently, Wm. Woonmos. Rev. Robert G. Hughes."—ln the speech alluded to Mr. Chamberlain admits that the onus of proof rested with the "Times," and added that the "Times" challenges Mr. Parnell to put it tothe proof in the only way that it is possible, and if ilr. Parnell shrinks to take up the gauntlet, an,l if he fears to face the ordeal of cross-examination every impartial man, every intelligent man, will feel that he has put himself in a position in which he is 110 longer a safe and proper ally for English states- men.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. H. Bleckly and Mr. T. Comber.

AssAturs.—Edward Price. potter, was summoned by Sarah Cosgrove, who complained that he assaulted her on the 10th inst. Defendant admitted having struck Mrs. Cosgrove, but alleged that he had received provocation. He was fined lOs and costs. A SLEEPY CARTER.—William Baines pleaded guilty to having been asleep while in charge of a horse and cart, at Sankey, on the 6th inst, and was ordered to pay the costs of the case.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. W. Long and Mr. C. Lister. ADULTERATED BUTTER.—William Shuttleworth, grocer, Lymm, was charged with havieg sold butter which was not of the nature and substance demanded, on the 1911 April.— P.C. Sumner stated that on the day mentioned he went into Mr. Sr.uttleworth's shop and lAught half a pound at is per lb, and 20z. of coffee, being served by a boy.—Superintene dent Leighton deposed that the butter had been forwarded to an analyst, who certified that it contained 80 per cent of foreign fat.—ln defence, it was stated that the boy who was in the shop ought to have mentioned that it was butterine he was selling. It was bought as containing 50 per cent, from a firm in Manchester.—A fine of 10s and costs was im- posed, in all 355.

Wigan won the toss, and the first tour wickets fell rapidly for 30 runs. McClure and McConnell played carefully, though the first ought to have bsen run out before scoring. Clarke fielded the ball smartly but threw in wide, and McClure got in. Denton was bowling grandly, and had so far, three wickets- for ten runs in six overt% McClure was taken at 84 from a rnis-hit, and McLeod joined McConnell, but only to get caught on the boundary by S. M. Crosfield from a big hit. The three last players kept up their wickets for a long time, and scored 90 runs. The total reached 230, Clegg not out 39. The Warrington fielding was ni.t near so clean and smart as usual, and several chances were missed, which, if taken, would have kept the score much lower. Denton ob- tained six wickets. Warrington bad a little over an bone to play. and two wickets fell to McConnell quickly. J. J. CroQfield and Denton made a stand, and carried the score from sto 46, when the former put a bumper back to the bowler. McConnell was getting the ball to rise fast off the hard wicket, and bit the next comer, Clarke, twice on the body. Denton was caught at wicket at 50, and Woodbead joined Clarke. Runs were put on at a great rate, and in the last 25 minutes 65 rune were scored. McLeod gave way to Armstrong, and tried the opposite end. In the last over Armstrong was hit for four fours by Clarke whose score in- cluded 8 fours, 2 threes, and singles. McConnell was the most successful bowler with three wickets for 34 runs. Under this heading "The Ironmonger" of last week gives an article which substantiates, with evidence culled from the reports of Government inspectors, raiich that has been said with regard to the oppression and suffering of the chainmakers at Oradley Heath and other places. The following is a portion of the article referred to :—" In his 1 annual report for 1886, the Chief Inspector of Fac- tories and Workshops, Mr. Alexander Redgrave, again refers to the manner in which the enactments of the Truck Act are subtly evaded in the chain and nail districts of Staffordshire, Warwickshire, and Worcestershire. In his last annual report Mr. Red- grave pointed out that there existed no 'giving of lines' (as in Scotland), and no direct compulsion, but it was well known, he said, that work would be only given to those who would silently accept it on the only terms upon which it would be given by the employers. Mr. Redgrave then pointed out that in no case during his inquiry would a work- man acknowledge that he was in any way coerced to deal for gleeds or provisions at any particular shop or warehouse. Mr. Redgra.ve now states that there has been no alteration in the system,the modus operandi of which is thus described by one of his assistant inspectors :—" A workman will go to the wirehouee and ask if there is any Nvork for him. Employer will say, 'l've an order here; I suppose you will want a load of gleeds.' If the workman refuses the , gleeds, he may get that order, but will be refused the next. A chainmaker informed me this week that he paid his master 15s for gleeds which he could buy for 78. The enormous profits made"' by the employers out of the gleeds enables them to Sell the common chains at cost price or nearly so, the system thus acting in a double sense against the workman, who will in addition get fined for any 1 links the least faulty. Workmen giving this infor- mation uniting add you won't say as I have said anything; if you do I shall be ruined.' The work- men hold that they have to work under these hard conditions br have no work at all. Mr. Redgrave. says it has been impressed upon the worktnen again and again that they have the remedy in their own hands, but the remedy is so severe and the result so certain to be detrimental that individual action is powerless, and it would require such an amount of courage in an individual that 'it can hardly be expected from one man to fight single- handed the battle of hundreds. The result is that the wretched system is still in vogue and is regularly practised, consequently the workmen are robbed and kept miserably poor whilst the trade is demoralised by the persistent underselling of the truck-masters."

THE LOSS OF THE STEAMER JOHN

KNOX AND 29 LIVES. Particulars have been received of the terrible disaster to the steamer John Knox, whilst on a voyage from Liverpool and Glasgow to Canada, and by which the whole of her crew. 29 in number, perished. The steamer was wrecked at the entrance of Channel Har- bour, Newfoundland, on the Ist inst. It appears that very early in the morning Hie inhabitants of that place were roused from their sleep by the •loud blowing of a ship's horn. On reaching the beach they saw through the fog and darkness rockets fired from a vessel in distress on the rocks on the south-west island. The sea was running mountains high and a gale blowing. So dangerous was the weather that a boat could not have lived in such a sea. The cries of the helpless sailors could be distinctly heard, as the vessel was only about 400 yards from the land. Nothing could be done, however, to save them, and it did not take the sea and wind long to perform their terrible work. The cries of the men grew fainter and less frequent, and then ceased altogether. At daybreak the weather had abated so ranch that a few fishermen put out In a boat, and found that the ill-fated vessel was the John Knox, with a cargo of iron, bricks, and liquors. Not one of the crew, however, was left to tell the sad tale of the ship- wreck, The crew numbered 29, and the fishermen recovered the bodies of Captain Brolly and 15 of the crew, amongst the latter being John 111‘Guire, a fireman, whose name was ascertained by a seaman's discharge in his pocket. Efforts were subsequently made to find the.other bodies. Those landed presented a melancholy spectacle as they were lying awaiting interment.

F.KECUTION FOR CHILD MURDER.

Henry William Young, a shoemaker, aged 27, was shoemaker, was executed at Dorchester on Monday, for the murder of his wife's illegitimate child, at Poole, under very brutal circumstances, last February. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner. The culprit:, who had lost a leg by an accident when a child, was visited by his relatives during the week, to whom, in the presence of the chaplain, he made a full confession of his crime. Although by no means, till within a few days of the execution, resined to his fate, the culprit had been most attentive to the ministrations of the chaplain. At times he was very much depressed,, and frequently gave way to outbreaks of grief, in which he bitterly reproached his wife for her conduct; but on Sunday, after partaking of Holy Communion, he became more recon- ciled, and frequently expressed himself ready. He passed a good night, and on rising partook of a hearty break- fast. The chaplain was early in attendance, and Holy Communion was again administered. Shortly before eight o'clock, Berry was introduced, and the process of pinioning 9peedily accomplished. The prisoner, who was very pallid, but did not utter a word, walked firmly to the scaffold, which was erected in an outbuilding to the rear of the prison, the doors of which were closed as soon as the procession reached the interior. The culprit took his place under the beam without flinching, the bolt was drawn as the clock struck eight, and he died without a struggle. A drop of six feet was allowed. Reporters were admitted, but the whole proceedings only occupied three minutes and ,a half from the time that Berry entered the cell. Young left behind him a bitter warning to men to beware of his fate.

In the Nisi Prins Court at Liverpool, on Wednesday, a Garston coppersmith named Billingsley and his wife recov- ered AIM from the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnehire Railway Company, as compensation for injuries they re- ceived in the accident at Penistone last September. MURDER OF A SWEETHELRT.—On Wednesday afternoon, in the coffee-room of en hotel in Preston, a young man named Alfred Sowery, pawnlsrokeris assistant, murdered his sweetheart, Annie Kelly, by shooting her in the head. The couple entered the hotel together and ortlend dinner,, and a few minutes later a revolver shot was heard. Kelly was found retilining in a chair dying from a bullet wound in the temple, and Sowery was standing near her with a six-cham- bered revolver pressed to his own head, and apparently try- ing to shoot himself. The pistol, however, had been ren- dered useless by the first explosion, and :,owery was seizcxl and disarmed Tne girl Kelly died very shortly afterwards. She and her murderer, it is said, had been "keeping com- pany" for several Jnonthe, and. had actually arranged to get married on Wedoesday, end leave on Thursday for America. Sowery when arrested had in his pockets £5O, with which he purposed defraying the expenses of the journey. On Thursday an inquest was held on the body of the girl Kelly, and the murderer, Alfred Sowery, was pre- sent in charge of a police officer. A number of witnesses were called, but their testimony added dttlA to What was already.known. The jury returned a veid.ct of wilful mur- der against Sowery, who will be tried at Lancaster Assizes. It has been ascertained that he and Kelly were in Liver- pool together on .und iy night, but there is no suggestion of impropriety in their relations. The marriage, which had been arranged for Wednesday, did not take place, and it is now mentioned, as offering some motive for the crime, that Kelly absolutely refused to cross the Atlantic with Sowery, , as he had proposed, until she had become his wife.

bell announces that, Mr. Smith has " iouriced," to rendezvous in the House, and by their numbers carry the Closure. To this point of purely me- chameal Piogress is legislation to-day come in the House of Commons. There is a good deal of gossip current touching the relations of old colleagues on the front 'Oppo- sition bench. It is said that Mr. Gladstone has cut Lord liartington, is not on speaking terms with Mr. Chamberlain, and scowls at Sir Henry Janice. 'All this is pure invention. ' Naturally enough ' the for- mer cordial intercourse is interrupted. But the or- dinary courtesies of daily life are preserved, and on • the front Opposition bench Mr. Gladstone and his old colleagues exchange remarks on the state of the weather and matters of similar engrossing interest just as if nothing had bappened. It is quite true that there is just now in the Dissentient Liberal camp a very bitter feeling against Sir George Tre- velyan, who has done much to weaken their, posi- tion. But here again there is no interruption of social intercourse. On Tuesday night, following his uncomprotnising speech at the Eighty Crub, Sir George Trevelyam I hear, met Mr. Chamberlain at dinner at the house of the editor of the "Daily News.,' Lord Rosebery was also present, and was well qualified to act as a peacemaker, if his services had been needed, but it is not likely that they would be called into request. The split in the Liberal party, as is • usual with the falling out of friends, has led to exceptional bitterness of feeling, But according to ' the wholesome rule of English 'politics it is not carried into the social' circle. Not the least interesting celebration of the 'Jubilee, and, perhaps, the most striking evidence of the far-reaching influence of the event, is the bell which the Reform Club is to give on Wednesday, the 15th of .June. The Jubilee of the Queen, by a happy coincidence synchronises with the fiftieth year of the life • Of the Reform Club, whence the younger spirits have been able to carry this bold scheme against the elders. It is not without a thrill that some whose term of membership goes back almost to the opening of the Club will read in the printed circular that "a part of the'club house will be set apart for dancing, and supper will be provided?! There is no charge to members of the club, who, indeed, could not very well be shut out from their own place supposing they did not feel inclined to pay for a special ticket. There is, hoW- ever, to be a charge of half a guinea each for strangers, 'Whether ladies or gentlemen introduced by members. Each.member is privileged to possess himself of two tickets, which makes it certain that tini club will be crowded. There is, perhaps, no passion more deeply planted in the female breast than , the desire to penetrate th'e' mysteries of a club house. Here is their opportunity, and it will undoubtedly be fully availed of. The attendance of members is likely to be extensive. The novelty of the occasion, and the prospect of seeing Mr. T. B. Potter and other revered seigneurs leading off the mazy dance must irove irresistible. It is a long time since anything was heard of Baron Albert Grant. His palace at Kensington has disappeared,•and on its site has risen a hamlet of villa residences. Leicester-square should keep his memory green; but busy London has cultivated to the highest pitch the art of forgetting people. The baron made his splash, went under, and was for- gotten, lie has, however, just unexpectedly reap- peared on the scene. He always had a passion for dabbling in journalism, and has now started a weekly paper, which he prices at sixpene,e, and calls the'" Stock Exchange." In the first number, issued a week ago, he made a bold and, as it turned out, a successful swoop upon tramway property. Dealing with the London Street Tramway, one of the most important and prdsperous of the metFo- politan lines, he announced, withoilt qualification, that four years hence the MetCopolitan _Board of Works would, in accordance with the Tramway Act, be in a position to take over the property at the price of old iron and the second-hand rolling stock. People intimately acquainted with traniways know all about this. It is no new discovery, but has formed part of the calculation of tramway authori, ties for years past. There undoubtedly is in the Tramway Act something of the kind paraphrased by Baron Grant. But it is so drawn up as to be absolutely inoperative. Mr. Chamberlain was aware of it when dealing with the Electric Light Bill, and took care, in introducing a similar clause in his bill, to avoid vagueness and'uncertainty, with the result that he temporarily killed electric lighting enterprise. The main stipulation of the clause...which Baron. Grant has adroitly, used is that at the expiration of 21 years from the con- struction of the tramway thodocal authorities may acquire it upon terms of paying the then value of the tramway. But „there is only a small section of the London street Pramways which in 1891 will have reached a term of 21 years. It has been built in sections, one only Completed at the end of last year. It is a rare pleasure to find' some really useful result arising in State quarters from the Jubilee. Something good is to come out of it in the check that will be given to the reproduction upon our coins of the youthful face the Queen wore when she came to the Throne fifty years ago. As far as I know the English coinage is, the only one which goes upon the principle that the reigning sovereign never grows old. In foreign coinages, as it used to be with English prior to the present reign, when a new, issue was wanted, there was a fresh die pre- serving anew portrait of the sovereign at the par- ticular date. Here is obviously a rare opportunity of creating a sort of portrait gallery, representing the Sovereign at various ages. The Queen has, however, set her face against the disturbance of

Sir,—What are the Liberal ilttionisis doing ore going to do that they are ashamed of 2 Why should they invite ad- herents under a pledge od.'secrecy and strict confidence ? We know what they have done, and their action has been cendoned by their old confederates. They have deserted their party; they have been disloyal to their leader; they have gone counter to life-long political professions; they have adopted a policy which seems to mean abuse of Mr. Gladstone, and a desire to keep a Tory Goverment in and a Liberal Government oat. All this they have done, and yet their former colleigues have looked on in sorrow, but not in anger. They have had moreover the support and coun- tenance of eminent politicians like Lord liartington, Mr. Bright, Mr. Chamberlain, and his Sancho PAWLS, Jesse Coiling'; all the Tories, and a splinter off the main block of the Liberal party. Surely it is unnecessary to invite supporters with a promise of privacy and strict conft-

dence. How far does the secrecy of the new association extend? Will they have a sign and a grip like the Freemasons—known to themselves, but unknown to the rest of the world? Will their officers be designated by the letters of the alphabet will they have a P.M. and a P.G.M , and a P.I.G. and a M.O.N.K.—the latter to be the great mystery man of the order and the chief depository of it secrets ? Other politi- cal societies come out In the light of day, and are rather proud of the publicity. For the first time in recent history we have a secret society for the promotion of quite constitu- tional objets. But our old friends need not feat to come boldly to the front. We shall never regard our present estrangement as anything but temporary. They are not the men to herd with swine, and teed upon husks for ever. They will look back to their old home, and to their father's house. When that time comes they will find us eager to welcome them. There will be the 'jest robe, and the ring, and the shoes, and the fatted, calf, and no elder brother to find fault with our rejoicing ever the dead who are alive again—over the lost who are found.
