MAKERS. Sir,—Will you kindly allow the undersigned, on behalf of the Committee, to return their sincere :thanks to the pnblic of VVarrinstton, and to the subscribers generally for their generous aid in raising a fund for helping the Cradley Heath ebainumakers in their distress? We also wish to publicly thank the band and other artistes who so kindly gave their services on the occasion, by which, we may add, we have been enabled to forward £25. H. WHITHAM, chairman. C. BUNCH, secretary.

WARRINGTON GAS BILLS. Sir,—l a inclined to think .bat there is amongst the gas censurers a very large amount of deep dissatisfaction at the way in which gas bdls keep up to a high figure. It is of no use practising economy iu the burning of gas; you might just as well light up all round; your bill won't be one trifle less. During the past half year, with a view to reduc- ing expenaer, the strictest attention has been yiv^n in my house to the gas question, but it has all availed notbi,,g; the bill is as high as ever. I am disposed to think that Mersey-atreet wants overhauling ; and I know there is a prevailing opinion to tbis effect in the town. Wages are paid there such as are paid in no other establishment, and yet the result is unsatisfactory. There is no doubt at all that the convecting link betweeu the Council Chamber and the Gas Works wants replacing by aomething of a more go- a•head and active kind. Why is net the meter question gone into ? I have had mine at least a dozen years; at 38 a year it should be nearly paid for at least half a-doz.m times over. I suppose the older it gets and the more profitable to the Corporation it will become.—l am, yours, &c, GRIN AND ABIDE.

THE NEWTON JUBILEE MEETING. Sir,—l fully purposed attending the meeting held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday last, anent the above, but was prevented by a professional engagement, in order to make a proposal that the money raised for the above purpose should be applied to starting a cottage hospital for this dis- trict. There are four large works in the neighbourhood; I mean, the Vulcan, Viaduct. Print and Paper Works, besides several smaller oner, and yet in case of accidents the nearest hospitals at which accommodation can be always provided, are a Liverpool or Manchester. Surely we could not better celebrate our Sovereign's Jubilee than by corn- !wooing an institution which will benefit so very many in the district. In serious accidents it is always of such extreme importance that the sufferers should be attended to, as near as possible, on the spot, and the further they have to be carried, the less the chance of their immediate or ultimate recovery. The size of the hospital would I entirely depend upon the amount of money raised. How• ever small that was, it would still be sufficient to make a commencement. I feel sure the response to a request for subscriptions to this object would be much greater than for any other purpose. With due deference to Mr. Pardy and Mr. Legh, though we are all undoubtedly very grateful to the latter for his generous offer. I do not think this district is in urgent need of a recreation ground. We always have Newton Lake, and there is any amount of open ground where the children can play at football, etc. Apologizing for trespassing than far on your valuable space,—l am, etc., CHARLES J. MOUNCEY. 16, Haydock-street, Earlestown, 18th May, 1867.

WIDNES FREE DINNER MOVEMENT. Sir,—! beg to acknowledge 24 61 from two mothers at Hough Green through Mr. Hambrook. I also desire to sub- mit a report of the season's work. The work commenced on Christmas Day, when dinner was provided for 200. consist- ing of potato pie and plum pudding, in the Simm's Cross school. On the 13th of January the dinners were served up at or near the schools, and were continued five days each week until tbe Ist of April, during which time, with the Christmas dinners, there were 2.586 dinners given ; also four pairs of clogs. The number of children on the list was 51, one of which was an orphan, two father is blind, twenty-six are fatherless, and the remainder were children whose parents were in very neceseitons circumstances from sick- ness or want of employment. It will be seen that there have been fewer cases relieved this year than last. We were happy to find that the distress was not nearly so great this season as last Mere vigilance, too, was exercised in ad- mitting cases on the list. I think I ought to say that such was the interest 'mani- fested in the work by the teachers in the junior department of Warrington-road school and the caretaker that they not only rendered excellent service in waiting on the little ones, but they provided at their own expense 108 of these dinners. The income far the season, together with the balance in hand from last year, is £.15 10810 d ; also a quantity of goods. The expenditure for dinners has been £l5 Is lid, for clogs 9s, total £l5 IN lid, thus making the income and expendi- ture practically the same, for which on behalf of the little ones I tender sincerest thanks.—l am, yours truly, SAM. B. STRINGER, Leah Villa, Lower Walton, near Warrington. May 17th, 1887. P.S. —The bill of fare has been similar to last year, viz., potato pie, hot pot, ash lentil, and pea soup, atc.

THE DEEP SEA FISHERMEN'S MISSION. Sir,—May I call attention through your columns to this humane enterprise? It is perhaps comparatively unknown in this district, and I think it only requires to be better known to have the hearty support of all who have the in- terest of their fellow creatures at heart. The object of the mission is to count•ract the evil influence of the " copers " in the North Sea by the addition at a mission ship to each fishing fleet. There are, I understand, 12 of these trawling fleets, and as yet only seven have got the substantial assist- ance of a mission ship. Five, therefore, are required. The mission ship is, in fact, a floating church, library, hospital, dispensary, and meeting-room. There the fishermen's spiritual and temporal wants are supplied, and it is only those who like myself have seen the rough life endured by the brave men of Lowestoft, Yarmouth, and other fishing ports on the east coast that can form anything like an accu- rate idea of the blessing these mission vessels are to those poor "toilers of the deep "on the wild North Sea. Now my object in troubling you with this is to suggest that ar- rangements might be made with the committees of the ikhinchester and Liverpool Royal Jubilee Exhibitions to al'ow one or more boxes to be Placed in and about the buildings for the purpose of collecting funds for a new mis- sion ship. Amongst the thousands who will doubtless visit' the Exhibitions there will be few indeed who cannot spare a trite to this most deserving cause. Full information of the pirticulars of the mission may be obtained from E. S. Mather, Esq., Bridge House, 181, Queen Victoria-street, _London, RC.; but if you will allow me, I will briefly state here that the people for whose benefit this mission is are people who, I may say, could not well be done without; it is through their labours that a great quantity of the fish j consumed in Lancashire and Cheshire is obtained, and that those who live perilous lives for our benefit should I in turn receive some benefit from us is the opinion of yours, ic. ALEXANDER WADDELL. Sale, Cheshire, May 17th, 1887,

THE LATEST JUBILEE SCHEME. Sir.—l am very much obliged Is" Desideratum" for his kind answer to my letter. I hope and trust that this Jubilee echeme will prove a success, and that we shall be enabled to enjoy a half-holiday once a week. I am also (for my own part) very much obliged to Mr. Diggle for taking this mat- ter in hand. He has proved himself the friend of the shop assistants of Warrington. I think the meeting on Thurs- day night was a success, considering that we had not so i very much notice given of it. Mr. Roberts. n his speech, said he wished more letters bad been written to the papers on the subject, or something to that effect. With him I think that if more letters were writien more notice would be taken of it. It is a matter that will benefit hundreds of assietants—for there are hundreds in Warrington—and it will not do the least bit of harm to anyone, therefore I think we ought to have a half-holiday, and if every assis- tant of Warrington will use his bit of infleence—however small—l think that in the end we shall have one. We don't want even Sir John Lubbock to close the shops we can do that without Ina help. There are a few shopkeepers in the town who would not close at grlt ; but I think they

would ultimately close their shops when they found that keeping them ones did not do them any good. One shop- keeper in particular, that I know of, not only keeps his em- ployees late at night, but he even robs them of their half- holiday at Easter and Whitsuntide. Sir John's bill is a very good one for such people as him, but I think even he could be brought to close his shop earlier and give his em- ployees a half-holiday once a week. Therefore, assistants, every one of you, kindly take this matter in band. Perhaps 't you say you will say, "Why didn this on Thursday night." Well, for the simple reason that if I bad opened tny mouth "I should have put my foot in it," and perhaps upset the whole concern, so 1 thought it wisest to keep my mouth abut. Excuse me. Mr. Editor, for writing such a long letter, but it is a subject of vast importance to me, and hundreds more. Wishing a great success to this Jubilee scheme,—l remain, yours respectfully, ASSISTANT, Warrington, May 20th. 1887.

div.head: FLOWER SHOWS FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: FLOWER SHOWS FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,—lt has often occurred to me as being somewhat re- markable that Warrington does not possess a society having for its aim the encouragement of floriculture. In very matey towns such institutions 'lowish, and the dates of the annual flower shows held under their auspices are regarded as red- letter days in the local calendars, attracting thousands of visitors, and consequently bringing grist to the mill of the tradesfolk. I see no reason why a similar effort in Warring. ton should not be equally well recognised. Our town is singularly devoid of attractions, and while vast sums of money annually flow from the pockets of our local pleasure seekers into foreign channels, we get no quid pro quo, for the simple reason that we have nothing to offer. With a park—provided, of course, that its use for tbe purpose could be secured—admirably adapted for the holding of such carnivals, and railway facilities par excellence. it seems to ine that but to attempt would be to succeed. I have no doubt if a canvas were made funds would be forthcoming for preliminary expenses. Apart from pecuniary considera- tions, I believe floriculture has a tendency to elevate the character— " Looking through nature up to natures God."

And I am convinced that if a taste for cultivating " nature's jewels "—for window decoration for instance—could be in- stilled into the working classes, tidiness would take the place of squalor in many a bumble household. We are on the eve of celebrating her Majesty's Jubilee, but we in Warring- ton are about to do comparatively little towards perpetuatiag the event. Indeed, in this respect,were it not for the munifi- cence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, we should cut but a Berry figure. It is true the wall fronting the Town Hall is to be removed, but this cannot be regarded as an act of perpetuity, excepting from Paddy's standpoint, seeing that it is a de- molishing process. Wby not found a Floral and Horticul- tural Society? Of course to organise a competitive exhi- bition in connection with the approaching festivities Is out of the question; nor, having regard to pecuniary considera- tions, do I think the occasion opportune for the experiment, seeing that every town and village will be occupied with its own affairs. But, at any rate, the ball may be started rolling. and if gentlemeri in the neighbourhood will give counte- nance to the movement and grant loans from duit conserva- tories, sufficient may be done for inaugural purposes ; and thus, while perpetuating in a happy manner an event unique in our national history, at the same time contribute a very pleasing feature to our local jubilee programme.—l am. sir, yours truly, T. H. C. 167, Bewsey-road, May 19, 1897.

WARRINGTON AND THE JIBILEE CELEBRATION. Sir,—ln my letter last week on the question of celebra- Ong Her Majesty's Jubilee' in saying that the life seemed knocked out of it as far as Warrington was concerned. I did not mean to convey the idea that the people of Warrington were net willing to show their loyalty (it will be the reverse if they can get the chance), but that the committee were not making the most of their position, not pressing close enough to those amongst us who are able to give. The nig- gardly way in which the school children are going to be treated, the unfortunate po,ition the teachers are placed in having to scheme and plan to make ends meet, and above all, associating the pulling down of the wall as part of the celebration scheme, are all having an adverse effect. I could scarcely have credited it, but it is a fact, that there is a widespread objection to a part of the money being devoted to that object, and that is one reason why the money that would be given ter an excellent school and old folks treat is held back. It appears then, to my mind, and lam judge. ing from the opinions expressed by leading gentlemen now, that it is not too late to retrace the steps taken, alter the programme, and go in for "A day to be remembered" by the children and old folks of the town, and that object only. The committee In their wisdom scrupulously placed the lowest sum possible for each child, sixpence per head; and at the same time made restrictions which could not be car- ried eut, viz, that no child should walk except those on the school register up to the end of April. Why, if the latter was carried out in its strict sense one half the children would not walk that will walk on that day. I say debar no child from walking on that day, no matter bow ragged it may be, and if it can get taken in by any school and par- take of what it may never have tasted before, a little bun- loaf, let it have it. Now, sir, what about the sixpence. I was going to try to divide it. I will do it in this way, and leave the committee to judge. On usual Walking Days there are schools who take charge of the children all day, and give them a dinner and tea; for dinner a Melton Mow bray pie, which costs at least fourpence, and then a tea. What then becomes of the sixpence here ? Other schools, who only give a tea, and are not fortunate enough to have a band, have to provide one which costs about seven pounds. Then there are flag carriers, tea makers, prizes, and sundries which you cannot get out of; therefore what becomes of the sixpence. The sixpence will net come in, and if it is to be the only sum allowed, it will be like "a farthing damages ;" the Sunday I schools deprived of their real pleasure walking day, sub- stituted for one of disappointment and discontent. What, then, is the remedy ? I say state no sum, whatever, per child. Let every school have their festivities as on Walk- ing Days, every care being taken against extravagance, the accounts to be thoroughly examined and taxed by compe- tent persons, presented to the Jubilee Committee, and by them paid. This. lam sure, will be the cheapest and simplest way of meeting the case. Let one thing be borne in mind, that the Committee instead of providing for I think they said 8,000 children, it will be more like 12,000. One word more. It appears that the schools are to get no help from Mr. Alderman Crosfield. His cffer to enter- tain the teachers of the various schools is all very well in its way, if it could be robbed of its political tinge, and very many will be regaled who fare sumptuously every day ; but I think I speak the mind of every teacher when I say that such an entertainment as this will not be welcomed, if by having it the children are to be deprived of the help which it is in the power of Mr. Alderman Crosfield to give —Yours truly, S. D.

div.p: 15 and 17, Wellington-street, Warrington, May 19th, 1887.
EXTRAORDINARY ASSA BOY AT DITTON.

On Tuesday, at Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Jus- tice Day. John Taylor, aged 21, labourer, was charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding Joseph Smith, a lad 13 years of age, at Ditton, on the 19th ult.—The prosecutor, who is the son of the station- master at Ditton, stated that on Tuesday, the 19th of last month he was walking towards Ditton Brook in search of ferns, when he found the prisoner lying on his back in a plantation near the brook. He asked him if he knew where there were any nice ferns, and the prisoner went with him. to the brook, and, point- ing to the water, said "What is that?" Prosecutor said he saw nothing, and the prisoner then pushed him into the water. Prosecutor seized hold of a branch which overhung the brook, whereupon the 1 prisoner took him by the throat and threw him back into the stream, and on two subsequent occasions when he attempted to get out of the water the pri- soner kicked him on the head and knocked him back. On the last occasion the prosecutor went under water, and when he came to the surface he found that the prisoner had gone. He managed with great diffi- culty to get home, and was put to bed, to which he was confined for five days by the injuries he had re- ceived.—The prisoner's defence was that the lad came up to him and said, "Tom, what are you doing there If you don't get up I'll stick you," and immediately afterwards stuck a penknife into his arra ; and that he then pushed him into the brook.—He was found guilty, sentence being deferred. On Wednesday the prisoner was brought up for sentence. His Lordship said that it was only in the providence of God that the prisoner was not on his trial for wilful murder. He hardly knew how to deal with such a ruffian. 11e had previously been con- ' victed, and he was a man against whom society must be protected. He sentenced him to penal servitude for twelve years.

ANNUAL DINNER OP THE COBDEN CLI:II3.—Mr. John Mor- ley presided at the annual banquet of the Cobden Club on Saturday. and delivered an interesting address. He drew attention, with an obvious meaning, to the attacks which the "Times" made on Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright, and quoted a letter by the right hon. member for Central Bir- mingham to the "great journal," in which he indignantly asked If the onus lay upon the accused to disprove the charges and insinuations against them. On that occasion Mr. Bright declared that it was no answer to say that the "courts were open," because the objects of the slander would scorn any tribunal but that of nubile opinion." Pee Chairman then quoted Mr. Cobden's remarks en the Irish question 35 years ago, and passA,d on to the subject of Free Trade. He believed that recent discussions had completely overthrown the Fair Trade and reciprocity men. He spoke hopefully of the condition of trade and commerce. There was undoubtedly depression. bat against this there were many reassuring signs. The" moral" of the address vas— forswear intervention in the affairs of other countries, make your artisans skilful and intelligent, stick to free exchange, push your commerce abroad more zealously, watch your national expenditure, reduce your debt, and conciliate Ire- land. Mr. H. Fowler M.P., commented upon the fact that with the exception of Mr. Ritcbie all the Conservatives in office were pledged to Protection. Representatives of France, Belgium, and New South Wales also addressed the assembly,

THE XAMINER. SkTURD Y, MAY 21, 1887.
BAZAR AT GREAT SANKEY.

Ye,terday afternoon a Jubilee bazaarwas opened is the Board Schools, Great Sankey, by Mr. W. Bet- mont, in aid of the fund for building new Sunday schools for the parish. There was a large attend- ance, chiefly of ladies. The stalls, three in number, besides the refreshment stall, were well filled with a varied assortment of valuable and useful articles, and the room was prettily decorated with flags and mottoes. The stallholders were as follows :-1, Mrs Ridgway, Mrs Jeans, Miss Fraser, and Miss Braide; 2, Mrs Whalley, Mr Percy Davies, Miss Smith, and Miss Pemberton ; 3, Mrs Houghton, Miss Jeans, and Miss Dignum. The refreshment stall was superintended by the Misses Litton. Among the gentlemen present at the time of opening were the Revs. E. S. Jackson (vicar of Great Sankey), Spooner (Widnes), Holden (Widnes), Messrs. J. C. Ridgway, W. D. Jeans, J. Cook, J. Whalley, Hat- ton, and Booth. 1 be Rev. E. S. JACKSON said the pleasant task be had got to perform was to introduce to them their old friend Mr. Bdarsont. It would be a work of supererogation to attempt to describe to them the rights and claims Mr. Beamont had to open a bazaar for a Sunday school. His werka—the works of a lifetime—explained that to them better than any words that could come from him. Mr. Beamont had been amongst them before to perform a similar task. They were then in a very considerable difficulty, having a church without a roof, and now they had got only the foundations of the schools laid. He might mention to them that they bad about £550 or £6OO either paid into the bank or promised, and that bazaar had been got up and carried to completion through the industry, activity, and self-sacrifice of some ladies who were present for the purpose of helping their fund still further. as there was a great difference be- tween £6llO and the £1,300 which was wanted. (Hear. bear) Mr. BICAMONT, who was received with applause, said he ' felt great pleasure in being present that day.:Sankey was a place which had a history, and when their friends from Warrington went to the West Indies he told them a story which redounded to the credit of Sankey. There was a gentleman living at the farmhouse where Mr. Hatton now lived who was a very celebrated man in bis day. He be- came the first governor of Jamaica governed the island far many years, and died there. Jamaica, name was Theophilas Lynch, and from him were descended the Cotton family, some of whom had borne the name of Lynch-Cotton. (Hear, hear.) They were a very grateful people at Sankey. He remembered reading that when in 1865 Mr. Owen had I been there a few years as the vicar of the place, and he had done bis duty so effectually that the people raised that beautiful church, of which their present church was the successor. Judging from the past he felt sure they would again do their duty in connection with that bazaar. He had great hopes they would be able to do something for the object which had called them together, and that they would show by the results that are produced that their labour had not been in vain. (Applause.) Mr. RIDGWAY, in the course of an interesting address, explained the eventS that bad led up to the present need for new Sunday schools. He also referred in eulo- gistic terms to the labours of Mrs. O'Brien in decorating the room. He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Beament for attending there that day. Mr. JSANS seconded the vote of thanks, and in doing so mentioned that Mr. Beamont was first admitted a solicitor in 1819, and that be was now nearly 90 years of age. The vote of thanks was passed by acclamation, and acknowledged by Mr. Beamont. The bazaar, it may be mentioned, will be opened this afternoon by the Rev. E. 4, Jackson.

IThen I object to the whole proceedings as irregular and improper, and most unjust.—The case was then proceeded with in the ordinary way, but at intervals Mr. Davies complained of the way in which Mr. Buckton examined the witnesses, and Mr. Backton com- plained of the way in whith Mr. Davies interrupted the Court. There was, however, no further altercation of any length.—Mr. Davies afterwards informed the reporters that his complaint was that his clients were remanded at Mr. Buckton's office on Monday, until Thursday, and not to the County Petty Sessions held on the Wednesday, they having been locked up since Sunday.

SALE OF WoRK AT WARRINGTON.. On Wedneseay afternoon a sale of work, which is being held in aid of a fund being raised to defriw the cost of a new organ, was opened in.Legh-street Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, in the presence of a number of the congregation and friends. Mr. John Platt, J.P., had been announced to open the bazaar, but he was unable to be present, and that duct VMS therefore taken by Mrs Rollason, of Simm's Ceoss, Widnes. At the commencement of the proceedings, the pastor, the Rev. R. Calvert, made a short address, in the course of which he re- marked that there was a debt of .£5O on the pre- mises, and the trustees were spending .£250 on the new organ and alterations. They could not yet say what the result of that effort would be, but an inti- mation was given a few days ago that they were not going to have any rest until the whole was paid, and the chapel, schoolroom, and organ were all free from debt. Referring to the increasing prosperity of the Primitive Methodist body, he said that it now had a membership of 191,641 per- Sons; it had 1,043 ministers, 16,120 local preachers,' 10,723 . class leaders, 41,132 Sab- bath schools, 61,339 teachers, 411,935 scholars, and 4,305 chapels, valued at £3,017,047. He WU sorry that the gentleman who had been announced as the one who would open the bazaar was not able t be present, but Mr. Platt had not forgotten them, inasmuch as he had contributed .£5 to the fund. Mrs. Rollason then declared the bazaar open, and the sale began. The following is a list of the stallholders .—No. 1 stall: Miss Calvert, Miss Midwcod, Miss Bissell, Mrs. Dale, Mrs. Throssell ; No. 2: Mrs. Bissell, Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Wakefield, Mrs. Titchett, Mrs. Proctor Jones; No. 3: Mrs. Cal- vert, Mrs. Richard Jones, Mrs. Midwood, Mrs. Loxley, Miss Jones, the Misses Crampton ; No. 4: Mr. J. Titchett, Mr. J. P. Jones; refreshment stall: Mrs. Swales, Miss Swales, Mrs. Pod- more, Mrs. George ritchett, and Mrs. Elwell. On Thursday the sale of work was opened by Coun- cillor R. W. Francomb, J.P., in the presence of a large gathering. Having been briefly introduced by the Rev. J. Calvert, Mr. FRANCOMB said that all great and good works could only be carried on with the aid of money. They were often told that battles could not be fought if the "sinews of war were not forthcoming, and neither could the great battle they were waging against everything that is wrong and in promotion of everything that is good. (Hear, hear.) He thought Mr. Calvert and the others connected with that chapel had done some- thing very useful in building the splendid organ in the chapel. He was one of those who believed that they ought to make places of worship as at- tractive as possible. They noticed that places of worldly amusement were made as attrac- tive as possible with the object of getting people inside them, and he thought every clergy- man ought to do all he could for the people inside the walls of his place of worship. If they attract the people who walked the stre2ts Sunday after Sunday inside their chapel by means of a beautiful and pleasant service, there was no doubt that the words they would hear would have an effect on their future life. (Applause.)—Mr. TAYLOR moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Francomb for opening the sale of work that day.—Mr. Taciiiirr, in seconding, said with reference to sales of work, that' he did not see any other method they could adopt that would answer the same purpose in raising money. He had thought that it would be a great thing if the churches would take the matter seriously into con- sideration and try to adopt some other method that would perhaps answer hater. He himself did not see what could possibly be adopted,as sales of work brought so many into active work. (Hear, hear.)— The vote of thanks was cordially passed, and Mr. Francomb briefly responded. We understand that the following donations have been received, viz. :—Mr. F. Monks, J.P., £5; Mr. J. Platt, J.P., £5; Mr. Rollason, ..E2 ; Mr. R. W. Fran- comb, £2. The sale was continued last evening, and will be again open to-night (Saturday.)

div.head: LATEST NE w s
div.p: LATEST NE w s

A rather mild shock of earthquake, lasting four se. coeds, was felt at Monte Carlo at eight o'clock on Friday morning. It is arranged that Mr. Gladstone will visit Cardiff on June 7th. Au address will bp presented from the Liberal Association.

Sir Henry Holland informed a deputation on Friday that the Imoeriai Government would not interfere in the dispute between North and South Queensland. The Central News learns that fourteen Provincial Cham- bers of Commerce have signified their intention of sending representatives to take part in the deputation to the Chancellor of the Exchequer on the Decimal currency ques- tion.

Too MANY POLICHURN.—At the County Waterford Pre- sentment Session. on Friday, the Justices and Cess payers unanimously refused to pass a presentment for the cost of extra police, on the ground that the ordinary force was sufficient to carry out the law. _ _

A BOATMAN'S':.,CICIDE.—On Friday morning, John Un- win, 45, a boatman, was found banging to a beam at the Finslev Coal Staithe, Barnley. He bad been drinking Since Christmas, and within tbe last few weeks bad broken up his home. Depression of spirits bad resulted. BIRMINGHAM MANSLAUGHTER CASE.—At Warwick As- sizes, on Friday Mr. Justice Hawkins passed sentence on persons convicted on Thursday of the manslaughter of Col. Fendal, at Birmingham. lhe woman Rooney, and her paramour Lester, were sentenced each to three months' hard labour, and the mother and father of Lester to one week.

Dnera SENTENCE.—AtIWarwick Assizes Henry Cowley. aged 65, a surgeon's assistant, and Henrietta Powell, mid- wife, were found guilty of the wilful murder of Elizabeth Harding, a dressmaker, upon whom they performed an illegal operation. Both prisoners were sentenced to death, Justice Hawkins promising to forward to the proper quar- ter the jury's recommendation to mercy. Tng PRESTON MIIRDRR.—The prisoner, Alfred Bowery, was brought up at the Preston Police Court, on Friday, charged with the murder of Annie Kelly. The court was crowded. The evidence was similar to that given at the Inquiry by the coroner. Sowery was committed to Lancas- ter Assizes for wilful murder. In reply to the charge he said he reserved his defence, and would call witnesses. Tun NAVIGATION OF THE D.—A large sandbank has accumulated below the shipyard at Connah's Quay, the largest port on the Dee estuary, and is becoming dangerous to navigation. At low water the bank is so high that per- SOLIS CAR walk across. The formation of this sandbank is exciting much concern at Connah's Quay, as it is apparent that if something is not done to remove it the river will be closed to shipping. GREAT FIRE AT A COTTON MILL —A fire broke out at Mr. Coddington's Wellington Mill, Blackburn, used for spinning, on Friday morning It started in the mixing room, and, aided by a gale of wind, the flames came through the windows and got into the upper portion. Two men beldhg- ing to the mill brigade were badly hurt when the roof fell, and were takes to the infirmary. The firemen worked hard and got the fire out by 11 o'clock, but not before the greater part of the mill was gutted. There are nearly 20,000 spindles, and the damage is about £16,000, and is covered by insurance. The mill was on fire about six weeks ago. IMPORTANT MEETING OF LIBERAL UNIONISTS. A meetiug of Liberal Unionist members of the House of Commons was held an Friday afternoon, in one of the Committee Rooms at the House of Commone. Lord Hart- iegton presided, and there was a large attendance, including Mr Joseph Chamberlain, Mr Richard Chamberlain, Mr Fin- lay, Mr John Bright, Mr Heneage, Mr A Elliot, Mr Caine, Sir Donald Currie, Sir Henry Havelock Allen, Mr Hobhouse, and Lord Lyrnington. After some discussion Lord Hart- ington was authorised to inform the Government that the feeling of the Liberal Unionist members was practically unanimous against the clause in the Crimes Bill under which cases could be removed for trial from Ireland to Eng- land. It was also agreed that, if any saternative was sug- gested by he Government, such propeeition would be con- sidered at a future meeting, A strong wish not to embirass the Government was expressed, and it was agreed to give a hearty support to any reasonable proposal which would have the effect of shortening the discussion on the Commit- tee stage of the Crimes Bill.

LIVELY SCENE BETWEEN SOLI- CITORS. A rather lively wrangle between two solicitors took place on Thursday morning, at the Occasional Court House, at Warrington, the disputants being Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, and Mr. Buckton, clerk to the county magistrates. On Mr. J. Tinsley, the magistrate, taking his seat on the Bench, Mr. Davies, who appeared to defend two men who were in custody on remand for felony, asked that the case in which he was interested should be taken first. Thereupon ensued a little altercation between Mr. Davies and Mr. Buckton, junr., who said that as one of the witnesses in the case in question was not present the application could not be granted, but the real tug of war came on at a later stage of the proceedings. Mr. Davies asked for the name of the witness, but was told by Mr. Buckton, junr., that he did not know it, and he (Mr. Davies) then left the room for a few minutes. Returning, he complained to the magistrate that the way in which he had been treated was unfair. GREAT GALE-DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY AND LOSS OF SHIPPING.

The severe gale which prevailed all over the country on Thursday night and yesterday morning had disastrous con- sequences in many places. Telegrams from Sonthsea report theta steam yacht drove ashore early yesterday morning, and that the schooner Industry broke adrift; the latter vessel will probably become a total wreck. Extensive fruit gardens near Canterbury were stripped of their blos- soms; Liverpool reports several yachts and pleasure crafts sunk, and the total loss of a landing stage on the Cheshire side of the Mersey; great damage was done to crops and fruit trees in Cheshire and other agricultural districts ; and damage to the amount of £BOO or MO was caused at the Manchester Conservative Cletb, by the fall ot a large chim- ney stack, which struck the roof, and fell bodily into the billiard room below. In Liverpool, a woman was seriously injured through the fall of a chimney:stack through a roof, and a boy named McKay was taken to the Infirmary suffer- ing from Injuries caused by the falling of a large gate. Snow fell in Leeds, and in Cheshire there were dense hail- storms.

div.head: AMERICAN RAILWAY TRAIN ROBBED.
div.p: AMERICAN RAILWAY TRAIN ROBBED.

NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—inteniKeRCR has been received here of a railway robbery on the Missouri Pacific Railway. A train when near M‘Neil Station, Texas, was stopped by marauders, who rifled the express car of its contents and robbed several paasengers. THE FRENCH MINISTERIAL CRISIS.

PAWS. FRIDAY—It is probable that MM. Rouvier and Deves will be included in the new Ministry. All other statements published by the newspapers concerning the Ministerial crisis are purely conjectural. The journals are much divided in their opinions as to whether Generale Boulanger shall be included in the new Government. The newspapers favouring his retention, howevel, are very paci- fic in their tone.

There Is no buoyancy In any department of the market, and the very strong tone in Liverpool has had no appreciable effect here. div.head: WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WIDNES.
div.p: WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WIDNES.

Of the ever increasing extension of the principles of Wes- leyan Methodism there is to be found another illustration in the Widnes district. A branch of the denomination was established in the village of Farnworth in the year 1849, when a chapel was erected there towards the cost of which the late Mr. Thomas Hazlehorst, of Runcorn, was the chief contributor. The cause has been successfully can ied on up to the present time, but the inconvenience of conducting in one building the Sunday school and the other auxiliary in- stitutions in connection therewith has recently become so great that the trustees have resolved upon the construction of a separate building for these purposes. With the object of raising funds towards the aim in view a bazaar was com- menced in Lacey-street School, Widnes. on Wednesday afternoon. In addition to Mrs Bolton, of Moor Court, Oak- amoor, Staffordshire, a prominent worker in the cause of temperance, who had consented to perform the customary ceremony, there were present the Revs. R. Burdon, J. Bry- ant, R. G. Hughes, D. Davies, and EL Owen, Messrs. B. Brown, F. Lawrinson, J. Robinson, R. Fogg, J. Houghton, R C. Taylor, S. B. Stringer, J. Peat. E. Warham, W. Clarke, S. Robinson, T. Robinson, W. Dainteth. T. Sadler, J. B. Cook (St. Helens), G. Davies, J. Peover, J. Stead tTarbock), J. Williamson, T. Hughes, J. Shores, senr., the stallholders, drc. In introducing Mrs. Bolton to the aseenablage, Mr. B. Brown adverted to that lady's honourable connection with the cause of tem- perance and to the amicable and friendly relations that ex- isted between her husband and his workmen. Similar feelings of cordiality existed between the employers and employed in Widnes, where they had not bad any wars between capital and labour which had done so much injury in some districts. Be was happy to say that there was a desire on the part of the employers to de all they could to assist the working-classes of the town. He hoped this state of things would continue, and that the efforts to educate the people both in learning and temperance would have the effect of elevating their moral characters, and thus make Widnes, although not the brightest spot in England. one of the happiest places to live in. (Applause.)—Mrs. Bolton, who bad a most cordial reception, acknowledged the kind remarks of Mr. Brown, and went on to speak' at some length on the advantages of total abstinence. She was glad to learn that a band of hope was to be formed in connection with the projected schools. She had mere faith in band of hope work than in any other form of temperance labours, as she considered that it was wise to found the education of children on temperance principles. (Applause.)—A vita of thanks was heartily accorded to Mrs. Bolton, on the motion of Mr. R. Fogg, seconded by Mr. T. S. Swale, and Mrs, Bolton having replied, the sale of the numerous beauti- ful and useful articles that were displayed on the stalls com- menced. Annexed is a liat of the ladies who bad to perform the most important functions of stallholders :—No. 1 : Mesdames Joseph Robinson, John Robinson, Stead, Fogg, Browning, Clarke, Hollins. No. 2: Mesdames Hedgcock, Lamb, and Harrison; Misses Hedgcock, Harrison, and Stead. No. 3: Mesdames Robinson, :veneer, Charles Rob- main; Misses Sankey, Emma Glover, M. E. Robinson. No. 4: Mesdames Burdon, Taylor, Stringer, Kendrick, Brown. S. Robinson, Swale, and Bray, and Misses Taylor and Brown. Sunday school stall : Messrs. Shaw, C. Rob- inson, B. Taylor, Lamb, H. Harrison, W. Browning, G. Browning, junr.. T. Hollins, W. Rylands. Refreshment stall; Mesdames S. Sadler, Bryant, Lawrenson, and Swin- dells ; Misses Sadler, E. Ward. Minnie Sadler, and Lillie internat. Various amusements were provided for the enjoy- ment of visitors.

The bazaar was continued on Thursday, when Mr. John Simpson, of Runcorn and Frodsham, performed the opening ceremony in the presence of a good company. After a few remarks from Mr. Thomas Robinson, Mr. Simpson delivered an address, in which he said that he always looktd back at his connection with Sunday schools with as much pleasure as anything he bad to do in his life, and believed that next Whit-Monday would be the 50th on which he had taken part with the Sunday schools of Runcorn. "(Applause.) Mr. S. Robinson proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Simpson, and announced that Mr. Joseph Cook, of St. Helens, and the members of his family, intended to subscribe £lO each towards the building fund.—The motion was car- ried enthusiastically. The total amount realised at the bazaar was £175.
SETTING A WOMAN ON FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
TWENTY YEARS PENAI. SERVITUDS.

At the Melees at Liverpool, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Day, Thomas Leyland, aged 43, collier, was charged with the manslaughter of a woman named Elizabeth Jackson, at St. Helens, on %the sth February. Mr. Swift cenducted the prosecution, and the prisoner was defended by Mr. Segar.—Mr. Swift, in his opening statement, Said that the prisoner and the deceased had lived together for eight years, and they had a child three or four years of age. On Saturday night, the sth of February, she was beard screaming in the backyard, 124, Duke•streer, and two men named Wilding and Cumming, who went to see what was the matter, found her in flames. They took her to her house, but for some little time the prisoner refused to let her in, saying to the men Take her away, she is not com- ing in here. Will none of you take her and keep her? Let the woman die." After the woman had been let into the house a doctor and a policeman were sent for. The unfiertunate woman then said, "My master set me on fire with a piece of lighted paper. He said he would set me on fire. Ile lit hie pipe with a piece of paper, and then threw it on me." The prisoner said, ‘• What do you say: do you say I set you on fire?" She replied, " Yes, you did, Tom." She afterwards added that he did it and would not put it out. The woman was subsequently taken to the hospital, where she died on the 16th of February from the effects of the burns. Before she died she made another statement, in which she tried to shield the prisoner, saying that he did not do it purposely. Evidence having been called for the prosecution, Mr Seger, for the defence, contended that this was a mere accident, and when throwing away a piece of burning paper the prisoner bad lit his pipe with, he ac- cidentally set her clothes on fire. He was naturally a some- what soft man, and when in drink, as seemed to be the case on the particular Saturday, he would not realise the danger of this careless action.—The jury foend the prisoner guilty, and recommended him to mercy, as he was a soft sort of man.—The Judge : There is not a particle of evidence that he is soft.—The police-inspector from St. Helens, in reply to his lordship, said that the prisoner was not of im- becile mind.—His lordship said the prisoner had been found guilty of manslaughter under most revolting and aggravat- ing circumstances. The jury had recommended him to Mercy, but for the first time—for he invariably took into consideration recemrnendations 0 juries—he could not act upon this recommendation. They bad taken the prisoner to be a weak man, because his counsel bad suggested it, but is his (the judge's) opinion the prisoner was entitled to no consideration. His lordship accented the story told by the woman that the prisoner threatened to put her to death and he had now done it. It was a case in which he must sentence the prisoner to 20 years' penal servitude.

GOOD TERTIARY. —The weekly session of the Rope of EarlOstown Lodge of Good T,mplars was held on Mon- day night, Brother T Martindale, W.C.T., presiding. There was a very good attendance. Several items of lodge busi- ness were transacted, after which the evening's programme —" A night with the poets and short readings "—was pro- ceeded with. An interesting selection of poetry and readings was given by various members of the lodge. During the evening Sister E Porter, D.V.T., of Liverpool, gave a brief address.

Sr. AUSTELL ELRCTION.—The counting of the votes polled on Wednesday in tke election for the representation of the t. Austell Division of Cornwall was commenced at one o'clock on Thursday morning and finished at five. The result was declared tobe as follows :

Mr. M'Arthur (G.L ) 3,540 Mr. Brydges Willyams (U.L.) 3,329 Majority The total number of voters on the register is 9,070, and allowing for double entries, abstentions, &c., it was expec- ted that about 7,000 votes would be recorded. The contest has been the most keenly contested in the county in recent years, and the importance attached to it generally has been shown by the number of members of Parliament who have assisted the respective candidates. Mr. Willyams, in addi- tion to being a local resident landowner, had the advantage of having sat for the borough of Truro and the Eastern Division of Cornwall, before the Redistribution Act. Mr. M'Artbur' who was returned for ths Buckrose Division of Yorkshire at the last election, but unseated on a scrutiny, altkough not locally connected, is a member of the well- known Wesleyan family, and the Wesleyans are a very strong body in the division. The polling passed off with- out disturbance, although there. had been some eicitement, and in order to be prepared for disorder, Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., having been stoned on Tuesday night, military have been drafted into St. Austell, and the peke reinforced. The division extends from the Bristol Channel to the English Channel, and, having very little railway communication, a great deal depended upon carriage accommodation, of which the Liberal Unionist candidate bad the beet supply. The result is therefore a victory for the Uladstonians. LAWN MOWERS. Garden Tools, Garde. Seats, Tennis and Cricket Outfite.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington—Ads.
